## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pucimandajātaka* (Ja 311), translated as *The Neem Tree*, belongs to the Pali Jātaka collection. According to its commentary, the tale is framed at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) near Rājagaha and was related by the Buddha concerning the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, beginning with the opening verse words *Utthehi corā* ("Robber, arise") [Fausböll 1883]. In the introductory narrative, a thief flees after breaking into a house near the city gate and seeks shelter in the elder's forest cell compound [Fausböll 1883].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a neem-tree spirit (*nimbadevatā* / *nimbrukkhe devatā*) who preserves the tree from destruction and thereby protects his home [Sahni 2008; Fausböll 1883]. Pragati Sahni discusses this tale in the study of Buddhist environmental ethics, noting that while the narrative portrays the Bodhisatta acting to save the tree, the underlying motive primarily concerns preserving the tree as an abode rather than valuing the tree for its own sake [Sahni 2008]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the spirit residing in the sacred fig tree (*assattha*) is identified as Sāriputta, while the neem-tree deity is identified as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].
